Never. The premise is a myth: glass at room temperature is an amorphous solid, and its flow is so slow that the timescale for noticeable sag exceeds the age of the universe by many orders of magnitude.

Old panes are uneven because of how they were made. Crown glass was spun into discs, producing uneven thickness, and glaziers often installed the heavier edge down for stability. Cylinder glass sheets had similar variation. Many old panes are actually thicker at the top or sides, which a flowing liquid wouldn't explain. Medieval cathedral glass that's nearly 1,000 years old also shows no measurable sag, and ancient glass lenses and artifacts keep their precise shapes.

Your modern float-glass windows are uniformly flat and will stay that way.
